title: Civilian Clothes
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 32 of 40
content:
Danse owned exactly one outfit that was not Brotherhood-issued.

It was ugly.

I loved it immediately.

He emerged from the back room at Bravo wearing faded work pants, a brown shirt, and a pre-War jacket we had traded for at Bunker Hill. Without the uniform, without armor, without rank insignia, he looked like an entirely different man.

He looked deeply uncomfortable.

“Well?” he asked.

I stared.

“That bad?”

“No.”

“You’re staring.”

“I do that sometimes.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Immensely.”

He looked down at himself.

“The jacket is impractical.”

“It has pockets.”

“Not enough.”

“No garment has enough pockets for you.”

“That’s a design failure.”

We were going to Diamond City.

Danse had resisted for days because the Brotherhood still operated nearby and because being recognized felt dangerous.

But Bravo needed supplies. More importantly, Danse needed to walk through a place where nobody cared about his former rank.

The market was crowded.

He stayed close.

Not protectively this time.

Uneasily.

People bumped him without apology. Vendors yelled prices. A child nearly ran into him carrying noodles.

Danse looked more overwhelmed than he had during some firefights.

“You all right?”

“Yes.”

“Liar.”

“I’m adjusting.”

“To civilians?”

“To not having a visible role.”

That made sense.

A Brotherhood uniform told people what he was before he spoke.

Now he had to be only himself.

We bought ammunition, soap, coffee, and a new pan.

At a clothing stall, Danse stopped beside a dark red scarf.

I saw the look.

“You like it.”

“No.”

“You absolutely do.”

“It serves no purpose.”

“It keeps your neck warm.”

“My jacket does that.”

“Then it serves a second purpose.”

“What?”

“Looking good.”

He stared at me.

I bought it.

Danse protested for six straight minutes.

Then wore it all the way home.

At Bravo, he stood in front of the cracked mirror adjusting the knot.

“You’re smiling,” I said.

“I am not.”

“You are.”

“It’s functional.”

“It’s red.”

“That is a color.”

“It’s your color now.”

He looked at my reflection in the mirror.

“What does that mean?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s suspicious.”

I stepped behind him and fixed the scarf where it had folded under the jacket collar.

My fingers brushed the side of his neck.

Danse went still.

The mirror caught his eyes meeting mine.

The room changed.

I let my hand remain there.

He covered it with his.

“You know,” I said softly, “you’re allowed to keep things because you like them.”

“I know.”

“You’re allowed to look good because you want to.”

“I know.”

“You’re allowed—”

Danse turned and kissed me before I could finish.

It was not careful like the first time.

Still gentle.

But no hesitation.

His hands settled at my waist. Mine caught in the front of his ridiculous civilian jacket.

When we separated, I was breathing harder.

Danse looked startled by himself.

“Sorry.”

“No.”

He blinked.

“Right. No apologizing.”

“Correct.”

His forehead rested against mine.

“I like the scarf,” he admitted.

I laughed.

“That was harder to say than kissing me, wasn’t it?”

“Yes.”

“Hopeless.”

“Apparently.”

The next morning he wore it again.

He pretended that meant nothing.

So did I.

We were both lying.

Diamond City recognized him eventually.

Not everyone.

One Brotherhood caravan guard did.

Danse and I were leaving the market with a bag of coffee beans and two replacement fuses when the guard stepped from beside the gate.

His eyes moved from the red scarf to Danse’s face.

“Paladin?”

Danse stopped.

The title hit him like a hand against the chest.

The guard went pale as recognition became memory.

“Sir, I—”

Danse’s hand moved slightly toward mine, then stopped before touching.

“I’m not a paladin.”

The guard looked around as if saying the wrong thing might summon Maxson.

“I heard you were dead.”

“So did I.”

It was the driest thing Danse had ever said.

I nearly choked.

The guard did not know whether he was allowed to laugh.

Danse saved him.

“You should return to your caravan.”

“Yes, sir.”

He took one step, stopped.

“Sorry. Not sir.”

Danse’s expression softened by a fraction.

“Be safe.”

The guard nodded and left.

We made it outside the gate before Danse sat on a concrete barrier.

I put the supplies down beside him.

“You okay?”

“No.”

Good answer.

I waited.

“He looked afraid of me.”

“He looked afraid of the situation.”

“I used to inspect his unit.”

“You remember him?”

“Knight Vargas. Poor trigger discipline when he was nervous. Improved after his second deployment.”

Of course Danse remembered.

“He probably thought I was going to arrest him for talking to me.”

“You are currently wearing a scarf I bought because it was pretty.”

“That does not eliminate the possibility of arrest.”

“It substantially lowers the intimidation factor.”

He looked down at the scarf.

His mouth twitched.

Then he went quiet again.

“I wanted to ask how the Prydwen is.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“Because he would have had to choose between answering me and following his orders.”

I sat beside him.

“That was kind.”

“It was practical.”

“No.”

Danse gave me a sideways look.

“Still doing that?” I asked.

“What?”

“Renaming kindness so it doesn’t embarrass you.”

He looked back toward the city gate.

“Maybe.”

We stayed until the moment passed.

Then I picked up the bag.

“Come on. We still need soap.”

Danse stood.

“Two bars.”

“Three.”

“Why three?”

“Because normal people stock extras.”

“We are not normal.”

“Fair.”

At the clothing stall, the same vendor who had sold me the scarf waved us over.

“Got something for your man.”

Danse visibly regretted having a face.

“My—”

The vendor held up a dark wool sweater.

“Warm. No insignia. Actual sleeves.”

I touched the fabric.

Danse checked the seams.

Of course he did.

“How much?” he asked.

The vendor named a price.

Danse negotiated with ruthless precision until she called him a bastard and reduced it by fifteen caps.

He wore the sweater home.

Halfway to Bravo, rain started.

He pulled the red scarf higher around his neck.

I smiled.

“What?”

“You look like a person going home from the market.”

His brow furrowed.

“I am a person going home from the market.”

Exactly.

He realized what he had said a few steps later.

His pace slowed.

I did not comment.

Neither did he.

But his hand found mine.

The trip home took longer because Danse kept discovering that civilian clothing had consequences.

The jacket caught on a rusted fence.

The work pants lacked reinforced knees.

The sweater was, according to him, “thermally adequate but tactically irresponsible.”

“You bought it.”

“I was cold.”

“You negotiated fifteen caps off it like a military campaign.”

“Overpricing should be challenged.”

At a roadside checkpoint run by settlers, nobody saluted him.

Nobody called him Paladin.

A guard simply glanced at our bags and said, “Evening, Danse.”

He stopped walking.

The guard looked worried. “Did I get the name wrong?”

“No.”

Danse’s answer came slowly.

“No. You didn’t.”

We continued down the road.

A few minutes later he touched the red scarf at his throat.

“What?” I asked.

“Nothing.”

“You look like you’re thinking hard enough to damage the sweater.”

He ignored that.

“It was strange.”

“Not being called Paladin?”

“Yes.”

“Bad?”

He took several steps before answering.

“No.”

That single word seemed to surprise him more than it surprised me.

At Bravo, Danse emptied his pockets onto the table.

Two fuses. A screwdriver. Three screws he had apparently acquired without noticing. A folded market receipt. One bottle cap flattened almost perfectly round.

I picked it up.

“What’s this?”

“Trash.”

“You carried trash home?”

He took it from me, then hesitated.

“A child at the gate gave it to me.”

“Why?”

“He said it was lucky.”

I waited.

Danse stared at the cap.

“You kept it.”

“It was in my pocket.”

“You put it there.”

“Yes.”

He set it carefully on the shelf beside the detective novel.

The man who once catalogued only equipment had brought home a useless piece of metal because a child thought it mattered.

I decided not to tease him.

That was how much I loved him.

Before putting the clothes away, he caught his reflection in the cracked bunker mirror.

No armor. No insignia. Red scarf, ugly sweater, tired eyes.

He studied himself longer than usual.

“Recognize him?” I asked.

“Not entirely.”

“Do you have to?”

He considered.

“No.”

Then he smiled at the reflection, faintly, like an introduction.

The mirror did not give him an answer. It only gave him a face he was learning to claim without a uniform telling him what it meant.

That night he folded the sweater and placed it in the same drawer as his Brotherhood undersuit.

Old uniform beneath.

Civilian clothes above.

Not replacement.

Layering.

I watched him close the drawer.

“Red tomorrow?” I asked.

“The scarf is useful.”

“Sure.”

“It is.”

“Danse.”

He sighed.

“I like it.”

“Say the whole thing.”

“I like the red scarf you bought me because it looks good.”

I put a hand to my chest.

“Growth.”

He kissed me before I could get worse.

I considered this positive reinforcement.
